brief.topic: Four Counters, Three Jars, Fifteen Possibilities

s01: Four identical counters. Three labeled jars. How many different shares can we make?
Two here, one here, and one here is one share.
Moving a counter to another jar changes the share.
We care about how many each jar gets, not which counter arrived first.
Let us turn one share into a row.
Keep the counters in jar order, and place a divider whenever we switch jars.
Two counters, divider, one counter, divider, one counter.
Now the jars can disappear. The two dividers remember the share.
Slide a divider to the left edge. The first jar is empty.
Put the dividers together. The middle jar is empty.
Every arrangement still has a clear meaning.
There are six positions: four counters and two dividers.
Choose two positions for the dividers. The counters fill the rest.
Six choices for one position, then five for the other, makes thirty.
But choosing the same pair in reverse order changes nothing.
Divide by two. We get fifteen shares.
Each row decodes into exactly one share, and each share has exactly one row.
That is why we have counted every possibility once.
The trick is called stars and bars: objects and separators.
What if every jar must receive something?
Give each jar one counter first. Only one counter remains.
It can go into any of the three jars. Just three shares remain.
A small change in the rules becomes a small change in what we count.

scenes.narration:
Four identical counters. Three labeled jars. How many different shares can we make? Two here, one here, and one here is one share. Moving a counter to another jar changes the share.

We care about how many each jar gets, not which counter arrived first. Let us turn one share into a row. Keep the counters in jar order, and place a divider whenever we switch jars. Two counters, divider, one counter, divider, one counter.

Now the jars can disappear. The two dividers remember the share. Slide a divider to the left edge. The first jar is empty. Put the dividers together. The middle jar is empty. Every arrangement still has a clear meaning.

There are six positions: four counters and two dividers. Choose two positions for the dividers. The counters fill the rest. Six choices for one position, then five for the other, makes thirty. But choosing the same pair in reverse order changes nothing. Divide by two. We get fifteen shares.

Each row decodes into exactly one share, and each share has exactly one row. That is why we have counted every possibility once. The trick is called stars and bars: objects and separators.

What if every jar must receive something? Give each jar one counter first. Only one counter remains. It can go into any of the three jars. Just three shares remain. A small change in the rules becomes a small change in what we count.
